newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain economy seen over-rated now, but to improve.
newsitem.headline: Spain economy seen over-rated now, but to improve.

text.p: Spanish officialdom's upbeat view of the economy appears to outpace current economic data, economists say, but many are still confident that Spain's growth will pick up and unemployment decline next year.

"They are telling us the economy is picking up, but it's a forecast. There is very little to base it on. It's wishful thinking," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid. "The economy is weak."
On Friday, Spain announced that the unemployment rate rose in October to 14.08 percent from 13.82 percent in September, although the number of new jobs hit a record monthly high of 912,972.
Separately, the Bank of Spain estimated that third-quarter gross domestic product had grown about two percent, little changed from 1.9 percent in the second quarter.

"With the available data for this period, we estimate that year-on-year quarterly growth of real gross domestic product will have been on the order of two percent, not very different from the past two quarters either in magnitude or in composition," the bank said in its monthly report.
National demand could also have risen by two percent, slightly above 1.8 percent in the prior quarter. Private consumption was seen stagnant compared to the first half.

Economists said the comments from the report appeared more sombre than might have been suggested by the tone of Bank of Spain Governor Luis Angel Rojo or Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato just one day earlier.
"The economic situation is fairly favourable," Rojo told a seminar on Thursday.
Rato said the economy had entered a recovery phase in the third quarter, and added that the improved domestic economic situation had been aided by a recovery in confidence and in credibility.

Both emphasised that Spain was shaping up well economically for the key single currency tests in 1997, when it must meet stringent criteria on inflation, long-term interest rates, deficit, debt and currency stability.
There are no requirements on employment.
"The situation is good when the unemployment rate doesn't go down?," asked economist Gregorio Gomez.
"Financial markets are improving but I don't see that the real economy is going in the same direction and that is what is finally going to count for convergence," he said.
For Lumholdt, Rojo's comments were "suspiciously in line with the government. I smell a rate cut coming. He's talking the party line."
Still, many economists believe the Bank of Spain is right on track when it forecasts improvement next year.
The economy should end the year and begin the next "with more elevated levels of real growth that can be maintained medium-term," the Bank of Spain said.
"We are seeing an acceleration in private consumption that could lead us to a GDP of 2.5 percent or higher in 1997," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
The government is forecasting growth of three percent next year, while Rojo on Thursday said expansion would be around 2.7 percent.
"Overall, we are expecting improvement," said Antonio Villarroya, analyst at Merrill Lynch in Madrid. "We expect private consumption to pick up substantially."
